claim: Adgrf1 (also known as GPR110, PGR19, KPG_012, hGPCR36) is an oncogene based on high expression in numerous cancer types.
source: Recent research has shown that the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor F1 (Adgrf1; also known as GPR110; PGR19; KPG_012; hGPCR36) is an oncogene. The evidence is mainly based on high expression of Adgrf1 in numerous cancer types, and knockdown Adgrf1 can reduce the cell migration, invasion, and proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Knockdown of Adgrf1 can reduce cancer cell migration, invasion, and proliferation.
source: Recent research has shown that the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor F1 (Adgrf1; also known as GPR110; PGR19; KPG_012; hGPCR36) is an oncogene. The evidence is mainly based on high expression of Adgrf1 in numerous cancer types, and knockdown Adgrf1 can reduce the cell migration, invasion, and proliferation.
evidence: The claim references previous research findings about the effects of Adgrf1 knockdown.

claim: Adgrf1 is mostly expressed in the liver of healthy individuals.
source: Adgrf1 is, however, mostly expressed in the liver of healthy individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract and is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The function of Adgrf1 in liver has not been revealed.
source: The function of Adgrf1 in liver has not been revealed.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Expression level of hepatic Adgrf1 is dramatically decreased in obese subjects.
source: Interestingly, expression level of hepatic Adgrf1 is dramatically decreased in obese subjects.
evidence: This observation is supported by experimental data from microarray analysis and RT-qPCR shown in Figure 1.

claim: The expression of Adgrf1 in the liver is directly correlated to fat content in the livers of both obese mice and NAFLD patients.
source: The expression of Adgrf1 in the liver was directly correlated to fat content in the livers of both obese mice and NAFLD patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from mouse models and human patient samples shown in Figures 4 and 9.

claim: Stearoyl-coA desaturase 1 (Scd1) is a crucial enzyme in hepatic de novo lipogenesis.
source: Stearoyl-coA desaturase 1 (Scd1), a crucial enzyme in hepatic de novo lipogenesis, was identified as a downstream target of Adgrf1 by RNA-sequencing analysis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Scd1's role in lipogenesis.

claim: Scd1 was identified as a downstream target of Adgrf1 by RNA-sequencing analysis.
source: Stearoyl-coA desaturase 1 (Scd1), a crucial enzyme in hepatic de novo lipogenesis, was identified as a downstream target of Adgrf1 by RNA-sequencing analysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment with the liver-specific Scd1 inhibitor MK8245 improved the hepatic steatosis of Adgrf1-overexpressing mice.
source: Treatment with the liver-specific Scd1 inhibitor MK8245 and specific shRNAs against Scd1 in primary hepatocytes improved the hepatic steatosis of Adgrf1-overexpressing mice and lipid profile of hepatocytes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Specific shRNAs against Scd1 in primary hepatocytes improved the lipid profile of hepatocytes.
source: Treatment with the liver-specific Scd1 inhibitor MK8245 and specific shRNAs against Scd1 in primary hepatocytes improved the hepatic steatosis of Adgrf1-overexpressing mice and lipid profile of hepatocytes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: Adgrf1 regulates hepatic lipid metabolism through controlling the expression of Scd1.
source: These results indicate Adgrf1 regulates hepatic lipid metabolism through controlling the expression of Scd1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings including RNA-seq, overexpression, and knockdown studies.

claim: Downregulation of Adgrf1 expression can potentially serve as a protective mechanism to stop the overaccumulation of fat in the liver in obese subjects.
source: Downregulation of Adgrf1 expression can potentially serve as a protective mechanism to stop the overaccumulation of fat in the liver in obese subjects.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that Adgrf1 expression decreases in obese subjects and that overexpression worsens steatosis.

claim: NAFLD is the most common liver pathological condition with a worldwide prevalence of 25%.
source: Overstorage of lipid in the hepatocytes not caused by alcohol is known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which is the most common liver pathological condition with a worldwide prevalence of 25% (Cotter and Rinella, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cotter and Rinella, 2020.

claim: NAFLD accounts for approximately 85% of all chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease (CVD), and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
source: However, if left untreated, NAFLD accounts for approximately 85% of all chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease (CVD), and chronic kidney disease (CKD) (Allen et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: NAFLD may progress to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: In addition, NAFLD may progress to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Rinella and Sanyal, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rinella and Sanyal, 2016.

claim: GPCRs are the largest and most diverse family of membrane receptor that play important roles in regulating most cellular and physiological processes.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest and most diverse family of membrane receptor that play important roles in regulating most cellular and physiological processes (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: GPCRs are major targets for currently approved drugs.
source: GPCRs are major targets for currently approved drugs (Hauser et al., 2017; Sriram and Insel, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hauser et al., 2017 and Sriram and Insel, 2018.

claim: A few GPCRs have been shown to play key roles in NAFLD.
source: A few GPCRs have been shown to play key roles in NAFLD, and modulating their activities to ameliorate liver-related metabolic syndrome was proposed as NAFLD treatment (Yang and Zhang, 2021; Kurtz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang and Zhang, 2021 and Kurtz et al., 2021.

claim: Human Adgrf1 was identified by phylogenetic analysis based on highly conserved amino acid sequences of the GPCR transmembrane domains in 2002.
source: Human Adgrf1 was identified by phylogenetic analysis based on highly conserved amino acid sequences of the GPCR transmembrane domains in 2002 (Fredriksson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fredriksson et al., 2002.

claim: Mouse ortholog of hAdgrf1 was identified 2 years after human Adgrf1.
source: Mouse ortholog of hAdgrf1 was identified by the same research team 2 y later (Bjarnadóttir et al., 2004) and various splice variants were detected in deep sequencing experiments (Bjarnadóttir et al., 2007; Lum et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bjarnadóttir et al., 2004, 2007, and Lum et al., 2010.

claim: Overexpression of Adgrf1 was observed in various cancers.
source: In general, overexpression of Adgrf1 was observed in various cancers, and it was required to promote cancer cell survival, proliferation, and migration (Liu et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019b; Shi and Zhang, 2017; Bhat et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2017; Nam et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to cancer-related studies.

claim: Adgrf1 is required to promote cancer cell survival, proliferation, and migration.
source: In general, overexpression of Adgrf1 was observed in various cancers, and it was required to promote cancer cell survival, proliferation, and migration (Liu et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019b; Shi and Zhang, 2017; Bhat et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2017; Nam et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to cancer-related studies.

claim: Targeting Adgrf1 may represent a new therapeutic strategy for anticancer treatment.
source: Therefore, it was suggested that targeting Adgrf1 may represent a new therapeutic strategy for anticancer treatment.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on previous research findings about Adgrf1's role in cancer.

claim: Adgrf1 is required for proper fetal brain development and amelioration of neuroinflammation.
source: It was also reported that Adgrf1 is required for proper fetal brain development and amelioration of neuroinflammation (Lee et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2016a.

claim: Adgrf1 is predominantly expressed in health adult livers.
source: However, Adgrf1 is predominantly expressed in health adult livers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The function of hepatic Adgrf1 remains unexplored.
source: The function of hepatic Adgrf1 remains unexplored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Adgrf1 induces the expression of Scd1, which contributes to NAFLD.
source: In this study, we provide the first evidence that Adgrf1 induces the expression of Scd1, which contributes to NAFLD.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq and functional studies shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The repression of hepatic Adgrf1 expression is a potential protective mechanism of preventing overaccumulation of lipid in liver.
source: By HFD-induced NAFLD mouse model (Nakamura and Terauchi, 2013), it is also shown that the repression of hepatic Adgrf1 expression is a potential protective mechanism of preventing overaccumulation of lipid in liver.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data from HFD-fed mice shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Adgrf1 is mainly expressed in the liver of adult mice.
source: Remarkably, in agreement with previous studies (Ma et al., 2017; Prömel et al., 2012), Adgrf1 is mainly expressed in the liver of adult mice (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B, and citations to previous studies.

claim: GRP110 proteins were mainly detected in liver and kidney samples.
source: The Adgrf1 protein expression in those tissues were checked by western blot analysis. GRP110 proteins were mainly detected in liver and kidney samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Adgrf1 mRNA is mainly expressed in hepatocytes.
source: Our cell fractionation clearly demonstrated that Adgrf1 mRNA is mainly expressed in hepatocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During HFD treatment for 8 weeks, the expression level of hepatic Adgrf1 gradually declined and to almost undetectable level at week 8.
source: Remarkably, in agreement with the microarray data, during HFD treatment for 8 wk, the expression level of hepatic Adgrf1 gradually declined and to almost undetectable level at week 8 as examined by RT-qPCR analysis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The mRNA levels of the NAFLD-related marker Fgf21 were highly induced in the livers of HFD-fed mice at week 8.
source: In contrast, the mRNA levels of the NAFLD-related marker Fgf21 were highly induced in the livers of HFD-fed mice at week 8 (Figure 1F; Rusli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F and a citation to Rusli et al., 2016.

claim: HFD treatment did not affect the renal GRP110 expression.
source: Interestingly, HFD treatment did not affect the renal GRP110 expression (Figure 1G, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The hepatic, but not renal, Adgrf1 level is tightly regulated by nutritional status.
source: Collectively, the hepatic, but not renal, Adgrf1 level is tightly regulated by nutritional status.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of HFD on hepatic versus renal Adgrf1 expression shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overexpressing Adgrf1 in the liver of STC-fed mice did not affect body weight.
source: Overexpressing Adgrf1 in the liver of STC-fed mice did not affect body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), fasting glucose level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), fasting insulin level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), and homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Overexpressing Adgrf1 in the liver of STC-fed mice did not affect fasting glucose level.
source: Overexpressing Adgrf1 in the liver of STC-fed mice did not affect body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), fasting glucose level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), fasting insulin level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), and homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Under HFD treatment, rAAV-Adgrf1 mice gained more body weight than their rAAV-GFP controls.
source: However, under HFD treatment, rAAV-Adgrf1 mice gained more body weight (Figure 2D) and body fat mass (Figure 2E–F) than their rAAV-GFP controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Under HFD treatment, rAAV-Adgrf1 mice gained more body fat mass than their rAAV-GFP controls.
source: However, under HFD treatment, rAAV-Adgrf1 mice gained more body weight (Figure 2D) and body fat mass (Figure 2E–F) than their rAAV-GFP controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher fasting glucose level than rAAV-GFP controls.
source: The HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice also had higher fasting glucose level (Figure 2G), fasting insulin level (Figure 2H), and HOMA-IR (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher fasting insulin level than rAAV-GFP controls.
source: The HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice also had higher fasting glucose level (Figure 2G), fasting insulin level (Figure 2H), and HOMA-IR (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Worsened glucose tolerance was observed in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: Worsened glucose tolerance was observed in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by GTT data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Overexpression of Adgrf1 in livers significantly increased hepatic glucose production induced in PTT.
source: Overexpression of Adgrf1 in livers significantly increased hepatic glucose production induced in PTT (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by PTT data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ITT showed that the glucose levels in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice remained insensitive at 30–60 min after injection of insulin compared to their control HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates.
source: ITT showed that the glucose levels in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice remained insensitive at 30–60 min after injection of insulin compared to their control HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by ITT data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Chronic treatment of either ASO-Adgrf1s only lowered the hepatic, but not renal, Adgrf1 mRNA.
source: Chronic treatment of either ASO-Adgrf1s only lowered the hepatic, but not renal, Adgrf1 mRNA (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) levels.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Liver hepatocytes abundantly and specifically express the asialoglycoprotein receptor that binds and uptakes circulating glycosylated oligonucleotides via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: It is due to the fact that liver hepatocytes abundantly and specifically express the asialoglycoprotein receptor that binds and uptakes circulating glycosylated oligonucleotides via receptor-mediated endocytosis (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2021.

claim: Chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment for 4 weeks significantly decreased body weight in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: In contrast, chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment for 4 wk significantly decreased their body weight (Figure 3D), fat mass ratio (Figure 3E and F), fasting glucose level (Figure 3G), fasting insulin level (Figure 3H), and HOMA-IR (Figure 3F) in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment of ASO-Adgrf1s improved glucose tolerance, pyruvate tolerance, and insulin sensitivity in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: In addition, treatment of ASO-Adgrf1s improved glucose tolerance, pyruvate tolerance, and insulin sensitivity in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice as demonstrated by GTT (Figure 3J), PTT (Figure 3K), and ITT (Figure 3L) compared to ASO-NC controls.
evidence: This is supported by GTT, PTT, and ITT data shown in Figure 3J-L.

claim: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher circulating cholesterol (CHO) than HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates.
source: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher circulating cholesterol (CHO; Figure 4A) and triglyceride (TG; Figure 4B) levels than HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates, but their circulating free fatty acid (FFA) levels were similar (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher circulating triglyceride (TG) than HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates.
source: HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice had higher circulating cholesterol (CHO; Figure 4A) and triglyceride (TG; Figure 4B) levels than HFD-fed rAAV-GFP littermates, but their circulating free fatty acid (FFA) levels were similar (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level was decreased in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice compared to chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment group.
source: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level was decreased, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol level was increased in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice compared to chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment group (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol level was increased in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice compared to chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment group.
source: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level was decreased, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol level was increased in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice compared to chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment group (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment could lower circulating levels of the liver enzymes aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine aminotransaminase (ALT) in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice.
source: Remarkably, chronic ASO-Adgrf1 treatment could lower circulating levels of the liver enzymes aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine aminotransaminase (ALT), as markers of liver damage and hepatoxicity, in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1-NC mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The livers of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice were significantly heavier than the livers of their rAAV-GFP littermates and ASO-Adgrf1-treated rAAV-GRP110 mice.
source: We found that the livers of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice were significantly heavier (Figure 4F) and paler (Figure 4G, upper panels) than the livers of their rAAV-GFP littermates and ASO-Adgrf1-treated rAAV-GRP110 mice.
evidence: This is supported by liver weight measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: HFD-induced lipid accumulation within hepatocytes was substantially more abundant in the livers of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice than the rAAV-GFP littermates.
source: Consistent with these observations, HFD-induced lipid accumulation within hepatocytes was substantially more abundant in the livers of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice than the rAAV-GFP littermates as determined by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and Oil Red O staining (Figure 4G, upper and middle rows).
evidence: This is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: More fiber extension and larger fibrous septa formation were observed for the liver samples of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to the livers from rAAV-GFP littermates.
source: Moreover, based on the Masson trichrome staining, more fiber extension and larger fibrous septa formation were observed for the liver samples of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to the livers from rAAV-GFP littermates (Figure 4G, lower row).
evidence: This is supported by Masson trichrome staining data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Treatment of ASO-Adgrf1s for 8 weeks could improve the hepatic lipid profiles of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice in terms of CHO, TG, and FFA.
source: Like the circulating lipid profiles mentioned above, treatment of ASO-Adgrf1s for 8 wk could improve the hepatic lipid profiles of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice in terms of CHO (Figure 4H), TG (Figure 4I), and FFA (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Overexpression of hepatic Adgrf1 in mice is sufficient to perturb lipid metabolism and hence the progression of NAFLD, especially in obese subjects.
source: Altogether, overexpression of hepatic Adgrf1 in mice is sufficient to perturb lipid metabolism and hence the progression of NAFLD, especially in obese subjects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Scd1 is a key lipogenic enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs).
source: Among them, we are particularly interested in stearoyl CoA desaturase 1 (Scd1), a key lipogenic enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), such as oleate and palmitoleate, by forming double bonds in saturated fatty acids (Paton and Ntambi, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Paton and Ntambi, 2009.

claim: Increases in Scd1 activity are involved in the development of NAFLD, hypertriglyceridemia, atherosclerosis, and diabetes.
source: MUFAs serve as substrates for the synthesis of various kinds of lipids, and increases in Scd1 activity are involved in the development of NAFLD, hypertriglyceridemia, atherosclerosis, and diabetes (Kotronen et al., 2009; Mar-Heyming et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kotronen et al., 2009 and Mar-Heyming et al., 2008.

claim: Hepatocytes isolated from the rAAV-Adgrf1 group showed the highest lipogenesis activity.
source: Hepatocytes isolated from the rAAV-Adgrf1 group showed the highest lipogenesis activity, while those from the control rAAV-GFP group had lower activity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by de novo lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The lipogenic activity decreased in the hepatocytes isolated from rAAV-Adgrf1 mice treated with Adgrf1-specific ASOs compared to the control group.
source: Furthermore, the lipogenic activity decreased in the hepatocytes isolated from rAAV-Adgrf1 mice treated with Adgrf1-specific ASOs compared to the control group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by de novo lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is a direct correlation between the level of Adgrf1 expression and lipogenic activity.
source: In agreement with the RT-qPCR data mentioned above, the results revealed a direct correlation between the level of Adgrf1 expression and lipogenic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular CHO.
source: In agreement with the in vivo studies' findings, the overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular CHO (Figure 6E), TG (Figure 6F), and FFA (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid measurement data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular TG.
source: In agreement with the in vivo studies' findings, the overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular CHO (Figure 6E), TG (Figure 6F), and FFA (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid measurement data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular FFA.
source: In agreement with the in vivo studies' findings, the overexpression of Adgrf1 increased the intracellular CHO (Figure 6E), TG (Figure 6F), and FFA (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid measurement data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Increases in intracellular lipids by Adgrf1 overexpression could be completely repressed by ASO against Adgrf1.
source: Their increases could be completely repressed by ASO against Adgrf1 (Figure 6E–G) and partially repressed by overexpressing Scd1-specific shRNAs (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid measurement data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Increases in intracellular lipids by Adgrf1 overexpression could be partially repressed by overexpressing Scd1-specific shRNAs.
source: Their increases could be completely repressed by ASO against Adgrf1 (Figure 6E–G) and partially repressed by overexpressing Scd1-specific shRNAs (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro lipid measurement data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The transcription level of Scd1 is regulated by Adgrf1.
source: In summary, the transcription level of Scd1 is regulated by Adgrf1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from luciferase reporter assay and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Adgrf1 enhances the lipid accumulation by inducing Scd1 expression.
source: Adgrf1 enhances the lipid accumulation by inducing Scd1 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Chronic treatment of MK8245 improves various metabolic parameters including lipid and glucose profiles in various animal models.
source: In agreement with previous studies showing that the chronic treatment of this Scd1 inhibitor improves various metabolic parameters including lipid and glucose profiles in various animal models (Oballa et al., 2011), treatment of MK8245 lowered the body weight (Figure 7D), improved glucose homeostasis in terms of fasting glucose level (Figure 7E) and HOMR-IR (Figure 7G), and performance in GTT (Figure 7H) and PTT (Figure 7I) of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to untreated littermates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oballa et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment of MK8245 lowered the body weight of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to untreated littermates.
source: In agreement with previous studies showing that the chronic treatment of this Scd1 inhibitor improves various metabolic parameters including lipid and glucose profiles in various animal models (Oballa et al., 2011), treatment of MK8245 lowered the body weight (Figure 7D), improved glucose homeostasis in terms of fasting glucose level (Figure 7E) and HOMR-IR (Figure 7G), and performance in GTT (Figure 7H) and PTT (Figure 7I) of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to untreated littermates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Treatment of MK8245 improved glucose homeostasis in HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: In agreement with previous studies showing that the chronic treatment of this Scd1 inhibitor improves various metabolic parameters including lipid and glucose profiles in various animal models (Oballa et al., 2011), treatment of MK8245 lowered the body weight (Figure 7D), improved glucose homeostasis in terms of fasting glucose level (Figure 7E) and HOMR-IR (Figure 7G), and performance in GTT (Figure 7H) and PTT (Figure 7I) of HFD-fed rAAV-Adgrf1 mice compared to untreated littermates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E, G, H, and I.

claim: MK8245 treatment did not change insulin sensitivity as demonstrated by ITT.
source: But there was no change in insulin sensitivity as demonstrated by ITT (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by ITT data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: MK8245 treatment lowered the circulating CHO and TG levels almost to the levels of HFD-fed rAAV-GFP mice.
source: MK8245 treatment also lowered the circulating CHO (Figure 8A) and TG (Figure 8B) levels almost to the levels of HFD-fed rAAV-GFP mice, but there was no change in circulating FFA level (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: MK8245 treatment did not change circulating FFA level.
source: MK8245 treatment also lowered the circulating CHO (Figure 8A) and TG (Figure 8B) levels almost to the levels of HFD-fed rAAV-GFP mice, but there was no change in circulating FFA level (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The AST and ALT levels were alleviated in the MK8245 group compared to the rAAV-Adgrf1 littermates.
source: The AST and ALT levels were also alleviated in the MK8245 group compared to the rAAV-Adgrf1 littermates (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: MK8245 treatment partially reduced the liver weight.
source: MK8245 treatment partially reduced the liver weight (Figure 8F), degree of paleness, severity of fibrosis (Figure 8G), and lipid accumulations (Figure 8H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Treatment of MK8245 could improve the lipid profiles and alleviate metabolic dysregulation caused by overexpression of hepatic Adgrf1 in mice.
source: To conclude, treatment of MK8245 could improve the lipid profiles and alleviate metabolic dysregulation caused by overexpression of hepatic Adgrf1 in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Healthy obese subjects without NAFLD had lower Adgrf1 mRNA expression than healthy lean subjects.
source: Healthy obese subjects without NAFLD had lower Adgrf1 mRNA expression than healthy lean subjects, but obese NAFLD subjects had similar Adgrf1 mRNA expression level as healthy lean subjects (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a public transcriptome dataset shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Obese NAFLD subjects had similar Adgrf1 mRNA expression level as healthy lean subjects.
source: Healthy obese subjects without NAFLD had lower Adgrf1 mRNA expression than healthy lean subjects, but obese NAFLD subjects had similar Adgrf1 mRNA expression level as healthy lean subjects (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a public transcriptome dataset shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The expression level of Adgrf1 was positively correlated with Scd1 in the liver (r = 0.4635, p<0.05).
source: The expression level of Adgrf1 was positively correlated with Scd1 in the liver (r = 0.4635, p<0.05; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of a public transcriptome dataset shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Hepatic expression of Adgrf1 protein was higher in patients with severe steatosis than those with lower degree of NAFLD.
source: Immunostaining analysis demonstrated that hepatic expression of Adgrf1 protein was higher in the ones with severe steatosis than those with lower degree of NAFLD (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data from patient samples shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Adgrf1 expression level correlates to hepatic steatosis in humans.
source: These data collectively suggest that Adgrf1 expression level correlates to hepatic steatosis in humans as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The mRNA level of IL-1β was significantly higher in NAFLD patients than in healthy obese individuals.
source: Supporting the hypothesis, it is found that the mRNA level of IL-1β, a key mediator of low-grade inflammation during NAFLD (Mirea et al., 2018), was significantly higher in NAFLD patients than in healthy obese individuals in the GEO (Profile # GDS4881) (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of a public transcriptome dataset shown in Figure 9D.

claim: After treatment with either CCl4 or STZ, the expression of IL-1β mRNA in livers increased four- to fivefold compared to the respective value of untreated HFD-fed mice.
source: Remarkably, after treatment with either CCl4 or STZ, the expression of IL-1β mRNA in their livers increased four- to fivefold compared to the respective value of untreated HFD-fed mice (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The expression of hepatic Adgrf1 mRNA was significantly increased after CCl4 or STZ treatment compared to the untreated HFD-fed mice.
source: Notably, the expression of hepatic Adgrf1 mRNA was also significantly increased after CCl4 or STZ treatment compared to the untreated HFD-fed mice (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The Scd1 mRNA expression level in the CCl4 or STZ-treated HFD-fed mice was significantly higher than the respective value of untreated HFD-fed mice.
source: Additionally, the Scd1 mRNA expression level in the CCl4 or STZ-treated HFD-fed mice was significantly higher than the respective value of untreated HFD-fed mice (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Inflammation induced by either CCl4 or STZ treatment can increase the expression of hepatic Adgrf1.
source: These results suggest that inflammation induced by either CCl4 or STZ treatment can increase the expression of hepatic Adgrf1, in addition to Scd1, which is known to be involved in hepatic lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 9E-G.

claim: Adgrf1 is highly expressed in liver of healthy subjects.
source: The present study has uncovered a previously unrecognized role of Adgrf1 in regulating hepatic lipid metabolism. Firstly, we demonstrated that Adgrf1 is highly expressed in liver of healthy subjects, and hepatic Adgrf1 is required for regulating lipid content in liver of diet-induced obese mice by both gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hepatic Adgrf1 is required for regulating lipid content in liver of diet-induced obese mice.
source: The present study has uncovered a previously unrecognized role of Adgrf1 in regulating hepatic lipid metabolism. Firstly, we demonstrated that Adgrf1 is highly expressed in liver of healthy subjects, and hepatic Adgrf1 is required for regulating lipid content in liver of diet-induced obese mice by both gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The hepatic Adgrf1 expression level of healthy obese human and mouse are downregulated.
source: Secondly, we found that the hepatic Adgrf1 expression level of healthy obese human and mouse are downregulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mice (Figure 1) and human samples (Figure 9).

claim: The downregulation of hepatic Adgrf1 expression level in obese subjects is a protective mechanism to prevent over-accumulation of lipid in liver.
source: The downregulation of hepatic Adgrf1 expression level in obese subjects is a protective mechanism to prevent over-accumulation of lipid in liver.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that Adgrf1 expression decreases in obese subjects and that overexpression worsens steatosis.

claim: HFD-induced steatosis and liver injury were exacerbated in obese mice with high Adgrf1 overexpression level.
source: The argument mainly based on the findings that HFD-induced steatosis and liver injury were exacerbated in obese mice with high Adgrf1 overexpression level, and knockdown hepatic Adgrf1 alleviated the severity of obesity-induced NAFLD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Knockdown hepatic Adgrf1 alleviated the severity of obesity-induced NAFLD.
source: The argument mainly based on the findings that HFD-induced steatosis and liver injury were exacerbated in obese mice with high Adgrf1 overexpression level, and knockdown hepatic Adgrf1 alleviated the severity of obesity-induced NAFLD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: IL-1β and Adgrf1 expression levels dramatically increased in subjects with more severe NAFLD conditions.
source: To explain the observation that hepatic Adgrf1 expression levels in NAFLD patients were higher than in healthy obese individuals, the expression levels of key inflammation markers in different mouse models were measured and it is found that IL-1β and Adgrf1 expression levels dramatically increased in subjects with more severe NAFLD conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E-F.

claim: The expression levels of Scd1 mRNAs and protein were dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: Subsequently, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis to investigate the mechanism of Adgrf1's role in regulating lipogenesis and observed that the expression levels of Scd1 mRNAs and protein were dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice and repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The expression levels of Scd1 mRNAs and protein were repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: Subsequently, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis to investigate the mechanism of Adgrf1's role in regulating lipogenesis and observed that the expression levels of Scd1 mRNAs and protein were dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice and repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adgrf1 mediates palmitic acids to activate the mTor and Srebp1 pathways to promote fat synthesis in mammary gland tissues.
source: A recent study demonstrated that Adgrf1 mediates palmitic acids to activate the mTor and Srebp1 pathways to promote fat synthesis in mammary gland tissues (Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2023.

claim: Srebp1 is the key transcription factor for regulating Scd1 gene expression.
source: Here, Srebp1 is the key transcription factor for regulating Scd1 gene expression (Zhu et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2019a.

claim: The expression of Srebp1 mRNA was dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice and repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice.
source: Our RNA sequencing analysis also revealed that the expression of Srebp1 mRNA was dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice and repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice, indicating that Adgrf1 might regulate Scd1 expression via Srebp1 in the liver.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adgrf1 might regulate Scd1 expression via Srebp1 in the liver.
source: Our RNA sequencing analysis also revealed that the expression of Srebp1 mRNA was dramatically upregulated in the livers of rAAV-Adgrf1 mice and repressed in Adgrf1-ASOs-treated rAAV-Adgrf1 mice, indicating that Adgrf1 might regulate Scd1 expression via Srebp1 in the liver.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data and established knowledge about Srebp1's role in regulating Scd1.

claim: Pharmacologically inhibiting Scd1 by MK8245 was sufficient to rescue the key metabolic dysregulations caused by Adgrf1 overexpression in the liver.
source: We found that pharmacologically inhibiting Scd1 by MK8245 was sufficient to rescue the key metabolic dysregulations caused by Adgrf1 overexpression in the liver.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Scd1 global knockout (KO) mice showed improved insulin sensitivity, higher-energy metabolism, and more resistant to diet-induced obesity by the activation of lipid oxidation in addition to the reduction of triglyceride synthesis and storage.
source: Previous studies reported that Scd1 global knockout (KO) mice showed improved insulin sensitivity, higher-energy metabolism, and more resistant to diet-induced obesity by the activation of lipid oxidation in addition to the reduction of triglyceride synthesis and storage (Ntambi et al., 2002; Miyazaki et al., 2007; Miyazaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ntambi et al., 2002, Miyazaki et al., 2007, and Miyazaki et al., 2009.

claim: The ob/ob mice with Scd1 mutations had significantly reduced storage of triglyceride and lower level of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) production.
source: In addition, the ob/ob mice with Scd1 mutations had significantly reduced storage of triglyceride and lower level of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) production (Cohen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2002.

claim: Liver-specific KO of Scd1 was sufficient to reduce high-carbohydrate diet-induced adiposity with a significant reduction in hepatic lipogenesis and improved glucose tolerance.
source: Remarkably, liver-specific KO of Scd1 was sufficient to reduce high-carbohydrate diet-induced adiposity with a significant reduction in hepatic lipogenesis and improved glucose tolerance (Miyazaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miyazaki et al., 2007.

claim: Scd1 inhibition was proposed to be a therapeutic strategy for the treatment of metabolic syndrome.
source: Indeed, Scd1 inhibition was proposed to be a therapeutic strategy for the treatment of metabolic syndrome (Jiang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2005.

claim: Scd1 is highly expressed in various tissues, especially adipose tissues.
source: First of all, Scd1 is highly expressed in various tissues, especially adipose tissues (Ascenzi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ascenzi et al., 2021.

claim: Expression level and activity of Scd1 are very tightly regulated.
source: In addition, expression level and activity of Scd1 are very tightly regulated (Mauvoisin and Mounier, 2011; ALJohani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mauvoisin and Mounier, 2011 and ALJohani et al., 2017.

claim: Harmful consequences from inhibiting Scd1 have been reported, such as the inhibition of fat mobilization in adipose tissues, and the promotion of proinflammatory and endoplasmic reticulum stress by accumulation Scd1 substrates.
source: Harmful consequences from inhibiting Scd1 have been reported, such as the inhibition of fat mobilization in adipose tissues, and the promotion of proinflammatory and endoplasmic reticulum stress by accumulation Scd1 substrates (Brown and Rudel, 2010; Leung and Kim, 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Rudel, 2010, Leung and Kim, 2013, Liu et al., 2011, and Zou et al., 2020.

claim: Optimal level of Scd1 is required to maintain health.
source: These findings clearly documented that optimal level of Scd1 is required to maintain health.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from previous research findings about the consequences of Scd1 inhibition.

claim: The hepatic Adgrf1 may be dispensable in adults.
source: Secondly, in contrast to Scd1, according to the phenotypes of Adgrf1 KO mice in previous studies (Ma et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2016a) and a dramatic reduction in Adgrf1 in the livers of HFD-fed mice and health obese subjects, the hepatic Adgrf1 may be dispensable in adults.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies and the observation that Adgrf1 is downregulated in obese subjects.

claim: Targeting hepatic Adgrf1 is a potential safe treatment of NAFLD.
source: Therefore, targeting hepatic Adgrf1 is a potential safe treatment of NAFLD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inference that hepatic Adgrf1 may be dispensable in adults.

claim: Repressing Adgrf1 can also regulate the expression of many other lipid metabolism genes.
source: Thirdly, according to the RNA-sequencing analysis, repressing Adgrf1 can also regulate the expression of many other lipid metabolism genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Deficiency of Adgrf1 can decelerate carcinogen-induced hepatocarcinogenesis in adult mice.
source: Notably, recent study reported that deficiency of Adgrf1 can decelerate carcinogen-induced hepatocarcinogenesis in adult mice (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2017.

claim: High expression level of Scd1 is genetically susceptible to hepatocarcinogenesis.
source: Coincidentally, high expression level of Scd1 is also genetically susceptible to hepatocarcinogenesis (Falvella et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falvella et al., 2002.

claim: It is highly possible that Adgrf1 also accelerates carcinogenesis by inducing Scd1 expression level.
source: It is highly possible that Adgrf1 also accelerates carcinogenesis by inducing Scd1 expression level.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known roles of both Adgrf1 and Scd1 in cancer.

claim: The amino acid sequencing of Adgrf1 are highly conserved in humans and mice.
source: As the amino acid sequencing of Adgrf1 are highly conserved in humans and mice, targeting Adgrf1 may serve as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of NAFLD patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the conservation of Adgrf1 across species.

claim: Targeting Adgrf1 may serve as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of NAFLD patients.
source: As the amino acid sequencing of Adgrf1 are highly conserved in humans and mice, targeting Adgrf1 may serve as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of NAFLD patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and the conservation of Adgrf1 across species.
